365.title: Ki Tisa: even the sanctuary rests (Exodus 31:12–17)
365.hook: the building work stops for Shabbat; these verses are sung on Friday night
365.tomorrow: Ki Tisa: show me thy glory
365.howItsDone: V'shamru (Exodus 31:16–17) is sung in the Friday evening service, and in many communities it is also recited before the kiddush on Shabbat morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bezalel, the craftsman filled with the spirit of God. Your line was craft is spirit. What did you make with care? Today, the work stops. Day three hundred sixty-five.

Imagine the most important project of your life. Not a work deadline. A home for God. The plans have come down from the mountain, the gold has been collected, the best artist in the camp has been named. Everyone is eager. And the very next thing the Torah says, right after naming Bezalel, is: stop. Not forever. Every seventh day. Even this building, the holiest work there is, puts its tools down for Shabbat. And the verses that say so are sung in synagogues every Friday night, to a tune many Jewish children know by heart.
screen: `THE HOLIEST PROJECT THERE IS.` → `RIGHT AFTER BEZALEL: STOP.` → `SUNG EVERY FRIDAY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The passage begins with v'shamru, and they shall keep. In the JPS 1917 translation: "Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant." Then it calls Shabbat a sign between God and Israel forever, because in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day ceased from work and rested. The rabbis paid close attention to where this sits. It comes right after all the instructions for the sanctuary. Rashi says the point is plain: however eager you are to build, the building does not push Shabbat aside. And the Talmud goes further. When the rabbis listed the kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat, thirty-nine of them, they drew the list from the work of building the sanctuary: sowing, weaving, writing, building, kindling, and the rest. The labors that made a home for God are exactly the labors that stop on God's day. There's one more word worth hearing. When the verse says God rested, the Hebrew is vayinafash, a verb built from nefesh, soul or breath. Rashi reads it as catching one's breath, getting one's soul back. Even the Creator, in the Torah's picture, pauses to breathe. Jews sing v'shamru on Friday night in the evening service, and many say it again at the Shabbat morning kiddush over wine.
screen: `V'SHAMRU: AND THEY SHALL KEEP.` · `A SIGN, FOREVER.` · `THE BUILDING DOESN'T PUSH SHABBAT ASIDE.` · `THIRTY-NINE LABORS FROM THE SANCTUARY.` · then, large: `VAYINAFASH: AND HE CAUGHT HIS BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one project to pause. Settle, and breathe. Think of the thing you're building right now, the one that feels too important to stop. A job, a house, a plan, a cause. Picture setting its tools down for a whole day. Notice what you feel: relief, worry, guilt. Let it be there. Then breathe out slowly, the way the word vayinafash pictures it, as if you're catching your breath. If you keep Shabbat, you might choose this week what will rest. If not, choose a few hours. The bell holds the time.
V'shamru. And they shall keep: the verses about keeping Shabbat, placed right after the sanctuary plans, and sung on Friday night.
Your line: even the temple rests. Today, put one important project down on purpose, and let it wait without you. Day three hundred sixty-five.

366.title: Ki Tisa: show me thy glory (Exodus 33:18–23)
366.hook: Moses asks to see God, and sees only from behind, from a cleft in the rock
366.howItsDone: This passage, Exodus 33:12–34:26, is also the Torah reading for the Shabbat during Passover and Sukkot, so many Jews hear Moses' request several times a year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, v'shamru: even the holy building stops for Shabbat. Your line was even the temple rests. What did you put down? Day three hundred sixty-six.

Between yesterday's verses and today's, the worst thing has happened. While Moses was on the mountain, the people made a golden calf. Moses came down, saw them dancing, and broke the tablets of stone. Then came the long climb back: pleading for the people, pitching a tent outside the camp, speaking with God face to face, the text says, as a man speaks to his friend. And now, after all of it, Moses asks for one more thing. The boldest request anyone makes in the whole Torah. He wants to see God.
screen: `THE GOLDEN CALF.` → `THE TABLETS BROKEN.` → `ONE MORE REQUEST: SHOW ME.`

segments.voice: In the JPS 1917 translation, it's one short line: "Show me, I pray Thee, Thy glory." God's answer comes in layers. First, a yes: I will make all My goodness pass before you, and call out My name. Then a no: you cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live. Then a way through. There's a place by Me, God says, stand on the rock. I'll put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with My hand while I pass by. And then: "I will take away My hand, and thou shalt see My back; but My face shall not be seen." So Moses, closest of all people to God, sees only from behind. What does that mean? The Torah doesn't explain, and Jewish readers have never agreed. The Talmud, in Berakhot, says God showed Moses the knot of the tefillin at the back of the head: a picture, not a portrait. Maimonides says the face means God's essence, which no mind can grasp, and the back means God's ways in the world, which can be learned. And many readers have heard something quieter in it. In life, you rarely see God coming. You see where God has been. Only looking back, at a hard year, a rescue, a meeting that changed everything, does a person sometimes say: there. That was it. Moses doesn't get the face. He gets a rock to stand on, a hand over his eyes, and the view from behind.
screen: `SHOW ME THY GLORY.` · `NO ONE SEES MY FACE AND LIVES.` · `A CLEFT IN THE ROCK, A HAND.` · `SEEN ONLY FROM BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time, months or years ago, that was hard while you were in it. Don't relive the worst of it. Just walk forward from there in your mind, slowly, to now. Who showed up? What held? What turned out differently than you feared? Notice anything that looks, from here, like a hand over the cleft in the rock. If you pray, you can say thank you for it. If you don't, just let yourself see it. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tisa. The portion of the golden calf, the broken tablets, and Moses in the cleft of the rock, seeing God only from behind.
Your line: seen only from behind. Tonight, look back over today and name one moment that looks better from here. Day three hundred sixty-six.

367.title: Ki Tisa: the thirteen attributes (Exodus 34:6–7)
367.hook: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering", chanted on holy days
367.howItsDone: The thirteen attributes are chanted when the ark is opened on festivals in many communities, throughout the Selichot prayers before the High Holy Days, on fast days, and many times on Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses in the cleft of the rock. Your line was seen only from behind. Did a moment look different looking back? Today, what Moses heard as God passed by. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

On the festivals, when the doors of the ark are opened and the Torah scroll is about to come out, many congregations stop and sing the same words, three times over. On Yom Kippur they come back again and again, through the whole long day, until the final service as the gates close. They are not words people wrote. They're the words Moses heard in the cleft of the rock, as God passed by. Moses asked to see. What he got was something to hear.
screen: `THE ARK OPENS.` → `THE SAME WORDS, THREE TIMES.` → `WHAT MOSES HEARD.`

segments.voice: Moses has carved two new tablets and climbed back up the mountain. God descends in the cloud, passes before him, and calls out. In the JPS 1917 translation: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." It goes on: keeping mercy to the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin. Jewish tradition counts these as the thirteen attributes of mercy. Scholars have counted them in slightly different ways, but the number thirteen has stuck. Now, the story behind the custom. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah, imagines God here wrapped in a prayer shawl like a leader of the service, showing Moses an order of prayer, and saying: whenever Israel sins, let them say this before Me, and I will forgive. So after the golden calf, the people are given words to come back with. Notice something about how they're said in the synagogue. In the Torah, verse seven goes on to say God will by no means clear the guilty. The prayer stops mid-sentence, just before that line, so that it ends on the word for clearing, for cleansing. That was a deliberate choice by the rabbis, and the Talmud discusses it. And there's one more step. Another Talmudic passage, in Shabbat, reads these qualities as a pattern for people: as God is gracious and merciful, so you be gracious and merciful. The attributes are something to call on, and something to copy.
screen: `THE LORD, THE LORD.` · `THIRTEEN ATTRIBUTES OF MERCY.` · `GOD SHOWS AN ORDER OF PRAYER.` · `AS GOD IS MERCIFUL, SO BE YOU.` · then, large: `MERCIFUL AND GRACIOUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one quality and practice it. Settle, and breathe. Let the list pass slowly through your mind: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in kindness, true, forgiving. Which one do you have least of lately? Pick it. Then think of one person who'll test it today: a child, a coworker, a driver, yourself. Picture meeting them with that quality, just once. If you pray, you can say the opening words as they're written. If not, just hold the word you chose. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tisa. The portion that ends with the thirteen attributes of mercy: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in goodness and truth.
Your line: merciful and gracious. Today, practice your one quality on the person most likely to test it. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

368.title: Vayakhel: he gathered them (Exodus 35:1)
368.hook: after the golden calf, Moses gathers everyone together again
368.howItsDone: Jewish communal life is organized around the kehillah, and certain prayers, such as the Kaddish, Barchu and the public Torah reading, are traditionally said only with a minyan of ten.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirteen attributes, the words Moses heard as God passed by. Your line was merciful and gracious. Who tested your quality? Today, a new portion. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

There's a word in this week's portion that has already appeared once, a few chapters back, in the worst possible moment. When Moses was late coming down the mountain, the people crowded around Aaron and demanded a god they could see. The JPS translation says "the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron". That gathering made a golden calf. Now Moses is down, with new tablets, and the very first thing he does in this portion uses the same Hebrew verb. Same people. Same root. A completely different kind of gathering.
screen: `A CROWD AROUND AARON.` → `THE GOLDEN CALF.` → `NOW, THE SAME VERB AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The portion is named for its first word, vayakhel, and he assembled. In the JPS 1917 translation: "And Moses assembled all the congregation of the children of Israel." The root is three Hebrew letters, kuf, hey, lamed, and it means to gather people into one body. From that same root comes today's word, kehillah, a community. For centuries, a Jewish town's organized community has been called its kehillah, and old records speak of a kehillah kedoshah, a holy community. The book of Ecclesiastes is named Kohelet in Hebrew, the gatherer, from the same root. Now look at the two gatherings side by side. The first time, the people gather themselves against their leader, out of fear and impatience, and make an idol. This time, Moses gathers them, all of them, and the first thing he tells them about is Shabbat: six days of work, a seventh of rest. Then he asks for gifts for the sanctuary, from everyone whose heart is willing. Commentators have long heard the repair in this. The same energy that built a calf can build a sanctuary. A crowd isn't good or bad by itself. What matters is what it gathers around. That's why community sits so close to the center of Jewish life. Some of the most important prayers are said only with a minyan, ten adults gathered together. A community is not just people in a room. It's people in a room for something.
screen: `VAYAKHEL: AND HE ASSEMBLED.` · `KEHILLAH: A COMMUNITY.` · `TWO GATHERINGS, ONE VERB.` · `WHAT A CROWD GATHERS AROUND.` · then, large: `GATHER THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a good gathering. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people around you who don't see each other enough: neighbors, cousins, old friends, people at work who sit ten feet apart. What could bring a few of them together for something good? A meal, a walk, a visit to someone lonely, an hour of helping. Keep it small and real. Picture who'd come, and what they'd gather around. Then pick a date, even a rough one. Breathe with the picture of them in one room. The bell holds the time.
Kehillah. A community, people gathered into one body. From the same root as vayakhel, and Moses assembled them.
Your line: gather the people. Today, send the first message that brings a few people together for something good. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

369.title: Vayakhel: too much (Exodus 36:5–7)
369.hook: the people bring so much that Moses asks them to stop
369.howItsDone: Jewish charity, tzedakah, is often given through communal funds, and the story of the overflowing gifts for the sanctuary is read each year in the portion Vayakhel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kehillah: Moses gathered the people again, this time for something good. Your line was gather the people. Did you send that first message? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

Every fundraiser in history has the same worry: will enough come in? Every school bake sale, every roof appeal, every online campaign with a little bar creeping toward the goal. Now picture the opposite. The money pours in so fast that the people running the project walk into the leader's office and say, please, make them stop. There's too much. That has happened, at least once, and the Torah wrote it down. It happened in the desert, with a camp of former slaves, building a sanctuary out of what they carried.
screen: `WILL ENOUGH COME IN?` → `PLEASE, MAKE THEM STOP.` → `IT HAPPENED IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Moses has asked for gifts for the sanctuary from everyone whose heart moves them: gold, silver, bronze, blue and purple yarn, linen, goat hair, wood, oil, spices, stones. The text says they kept bringing, morning after morning. Then the craftspeople stop their work and come to Moses. The people are bringing much more than enough, they say. So Moses sends word through the whole camp: no man or woman should make anything more for the offering. And the Torah adds, so the people were held back from bringing. Then one last line, in the JPS 1917 translation: "For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much." In Hebrew that's dayam v'hoter: their enough, and more. Commentators have puzzled over it. How can something be exactly sufficient and also too much? The eighteenth-century commentator Or HaChaim offers a tender answer: there really was extra, but God made room for all of it in the work, so that no one who gave would see their gift set aside. There's a sharper note in the Jerusalem Talmud. It observes that this same people gave their gold for the calf, and gave their gold for the sanctuary. The generosity was the same both times. What changed was what it was for. And notice who says stop. Not the givers. The builders. It takes someone close to the work to see that the need is met, and the honesty to say so out loud, when it would be easy to keep taking.
screen: `MORNING AFTER MORNING, MORE.` · `THE BUILDERS SAY: ENOUGH.` · `DAYAM V'HOTER: ENOUGH, AND MORE.` · `THE SAME GOLD, A DIFFERENT AIM.` · then, large: `THEY HAD TO SAY STOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice enough. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are, slowly. The food in the kitchen. The clothes in the closet. The apps on the phone, the hours in the week, the people who love you. Pick one place where you already have enough, maybe more than enough, and simply say so to yourself: this is enough. Notice whether you believe it. Then breathe in, and breathe out, and let the wanting rest for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Vayakhel. The portion where Moses gathers the people, and they give so much that the builders have to ask them to stop.
Your line: they had to say stop. Today, when you reach for more of something, pause once and ask: is this already enough? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

370.title: Vayakhel: the women's mirrors (Exodus 38:8)
370.hook: the washing basin is made from women's copper mirrors; Rashi says God held them most dear
370.howItsDone: Rashi's midrash on the mirrors is a well-loved teaching on the portion Vayakhel, often cited to honor the women of the Exodus whose courage kept families alive in slavery.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a fundraiser that overflowed. Your line was they had to say stop. Did you find a place where you already have enough? Day three hundred seventy.

Before glass mirrors, people looked at themselves in polished metal. A disk of copper or bronze, rubbed until it shone, held up close to the face. In the desert, some Israelite women had mirrors like that, carried all the way out of Egypt. Small, personal things, the kind you might not think to give to a holy building. In the middle of a long list of what Bezalel made, the Torah stops for one sentence to say where the metal for a single object came from. The object is the washing basin. The metal came from those mirrors.
screen: `POLISHED COPPER MIRRORS.` → `CARRIED OUT OF EGYPT.` → `ONE SENTENCE IN A LONG LIST.`

segments.voice: The verse says Bezalel made the basin of bronze, and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the women who gathered at the door of the tent of meeting. That basin stood between the tent and the altar, and the priests washed their hands and feet in it before they served. The text tells us nothing more about the women. The Torah is silent on who they were or why they gave. Rashi fills the silence with a midrash, and it's a striking one. When the women brought their mirrors, Moses hesitated. These were things made for vanity, he thought, for looking pretty. Then God said to him: accept them. These are dearer to Me than everything else. Why? Because of Egypt. The midrash says that when the men came home crushed from the slave labor, these women took their mirrors, sat beside their husbands, made them laugh and look again, and kept love alive. Families kept growing, even in slavery. Because of those mirrors, the midrash says, a people survived to leave. So the very objects Moses nearly turned away became the basin where holiness began each morning. Notice the reversal. A mirror shows you yourself. A basin of water is where you prepare to serve someone else. The same metal did both. And the gift Moses almost refused was the one God held most dear. Sometimes the most important offering is the one that looks least holy.
screen: `MIRRORS OF THE WOMEN AT THE DOOR.` · `THE BASIN WHERE PRIESTS WASHED.` · `MOSES HESITATED.` · `DEARER TO ME THAN EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `MIRRORS BECAME THE BASIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an overlooked gift. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone gave that nobody counted as important. A mother who kept the house laughing in a bad year. A friend who sent silly texts when things were dark. A coworker whose small kindness kept a team together. Hold that person in mind. Name exactly what they gave, and what it made possible later. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If not, just let the gift be seen. The bell holds the time.
Vayakhel. The portion where Bezalel builds, and the women's bronze mirrors become the basin the priests wash in.
Your line: mirrors became the basin. Today, tell one person about a gift of theirs that others overlooked. Day three hundred seventy.

371.title: Vayakhel: wise-hearted spinners (Exodus 35:25–26)
371.hook: women whose hearts stirred them spun the goats' hair with skill
371.howItsDone: The phrase chochmat lev, wisdom of heart, is used in Jewish tradition for skill in crafts, and the women spinners of Exodus 35 are often remembered when the portion Vayakhel is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women's bronze mirrors that became the priests' basin. Your line was mirrors became the basin. Whose overlooked gift did you name? Day three hundred seventy-one.

Goat hair is not glamorous. It's coarse, it smells like goat, and it's hard to work. But the sanctuary needed it: a tent of goat-hair cloth stretched over the beautiful inner curtains, taking the sun and the dust and the wind so the rest could stay fine. Somebody had to spin it into yarn. The Torah could have just said it was done. Instead, it stops to tell us who did it, and how they felt while they did it.
screen: `COARSE, HARD-TO-WORK GOAT HAIR.` → `THE TENT OVER THE TENT.` → `WHO SPUN IT, AND HOW.`

segments.voice: In the JPS 1917 translation: "And all the women that were wise-hearted did spin with their hands." They brought blue and purple and scarlet yarn, and fine linen. Then the next verse: "And all the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom spun the goats' hair." Twice in two verses, wisdom sits in the heart. In Hebrew, chochmat lev, wisdom of heart, is the Torah's phrase for skill. The heart in biblical Hebrew is where people think and choose, not only where they feel. So a skilled hand starts in a wise heart. Rashi adds a detail from the Talmud that makes the scene almost impossible to picture. He says these women spun the hair while it was still on the goats. Whether it was a rare technique or a marvel, the rabbis wanted us to see a skill so great it seemed like wonder. And they're named right there in the building story, alongside Bezalel and the craftsmen. This was a week of what the sanctuary is made of. The building stopping for Shabbat. Moses in the cleft of the rock. The thirteen attributes. Moses gathering the people again. Gifts so many the builders said stop. Mirrors turned into a basin. And now, women spinning coarse hair with wise hearts, for the tent that would take the weather. The sanctuary isn't only gold. It's also goat hair, spun by people whose names we'll never know, and whose skill the Torah made sure to record.
